Langevin dynamics, grounded in the Einstein relation, is frequently employed to simulate polymer and protein conformations, even when applied to scenarios lacking equilibrium conditions characterized by spatial variations in temperature. This study investigates whether this relation holds in such non-equilibrium, position-dependent temperature environments. Our findings indicate that, unlike equilibrium cases, systems with varying temperature distributions do not generally obey the Einstein relation. Although the distribution of the number of steps taken remains unaffected by such gradients, the distribution of spatial displacement does differ from that of an equilibrium system. We propose an alternative approach to the unbalanced Einstein relation and validate it through the development of a new, effective potential that aligns both the mean and variance of the step-number distribution. Furthermore, this effective potential successfully reproduces the spatial displacement distribution; its accuracy is confirmed via Monte Carlo simulations. Although this effective potential is not strictly potential of mean force, it closely approximates one, exhibiting only minor deviations. Consequently, when equipping conformational sampling algorithms with this derived potential, the resulting ensembles match those generated by free molecular dynamics, though they diverge significantly from canonical Monte Carlo methods.

Various deep learning training strategies, such as label smoothing and weight decay (parameter norm regularization), have been observed to curb model complexity and enhance generalization performance. Yet, the relationship underlying these effects remains poorly understood. This study offers significant theoretical insights into this phenomenon by examining a linear model trained via stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in an overparameterized setting with $\ell_2$ regularization. We demonstrate that such training dynamics result in the convergence of the population loss gradient to zero before overparameterized equivalence eras are reached, thereby providing theoretical confirmation supported by existing empirical data.

Achieving precise measurements of physical parameters demands retaining every relevant detail from data sets, whether from natural processes or simulations. This study examines sideband events from $B^0 \to J/\psi K^{*0}$ decays utilizing the full kinematic profile to refine $B^0 \to J/\psi K^{0}_S$ parameters. By employing an unbinned maximum-likelihood fit on the invariant mass spectrum of $B^0 \to J/\psi K^{0}_S$ decays—where the shape of background contributors is derived from $B^0 \to J/\psi K^{0}_S$ events outside the signal region—we significantly enhance our ability to isolate genuine signal events. This method effectively counters non-linearity caused by background event shapes that, if assumed uniform, would skew results. Using simulations and the LHCb dataset from 2011, which collected $1 \text{ fb}^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data, we achieved a $4.1\sigma$ observation of $B^0 \to B^0 \to J/\psi K^{0}_S$ decays.

Recent advancements in large-scale data collection have enabled significant progress in Natural Language Processing (NLP) through Supervised Learning (SL). While SL algorithms excel in resource-rich settings, they typically underperform in data-scarce scenarios common in real-world applications, such as social media analysis or medical record processing. To address this limitation, researchers have developed various strategies to maximize the utility of small datasets, with data augmentation (DA) emerging as a particularly effective solution. Originally rooted in digital image processing, the concept of augmenting data has since expanded to other domains including speech recognition, machine translation, and sentiment analysis. This paper provides a comprehensive review of current data augmentation techniques and their applications within the domain of automated essay grading.

This work examines the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) and Lasso approximation for estimating parameters in causal models defined by marginal independence; it further demonstrates that both the MLE and Lasso are highly consistent, achieving the global optimum of the Lasso problem with probability approaching one as the sample size increases.

I develop an analytical framework for examining intergenerational patterns of social and economic inequality within societies. Rooted in this model are a set of assumptions regarding how opportunities are distributed, each carrying a specific degree of certainty. It further assumes that the placement of opportunities in any given epoch influences opportunities in subsequent eras. By analyzing the various possibilities, we can determine which outcomes are wholly inevitable, wholly variable, or partially fixed versus variable. The model ultimately provides a method to identify which consequences are partially fixed and variable, and to what extent they depend on chance.

We calculate the specific contribution to the energy of $N$-body wavefunctions arising from the exchange of identical particles within a general spherically symmetric potential, addressing both bosons and fermions. This calculation considers a set of the potential's quantum numbers ($n$, $l$, $j$, and magnetic quantum number) and incorporates the effects of identical particles up to $N=4$. We observe that the potential parameters, the principal quantum number, and the total energy of an $N$-body system can be determined with high precision by averaging the squared differences between the permuted coordinates of all identical particles. Furthermore, we confirm that the wave function for identical particles acquires a factor of $(-1)^{2j}$ (or $-1$ for bosons) when the coordinates of any two are swapped, a sign that corresponds to their spin. These findings suggest that the principal quantum number for an $N$-body system can be identified as the unique, positive-integer root of an explicitly defined polynomial equation. This same polynomial equation also yields the potential parameters required to accurately model the total energy of the $N$-body system.

The Monero cryptocurrency utilizes intricate adaptive ring signatures and confidential transactions (RingCT) to ensure total user anonymity, though this complexity results in substantial bloating of the transaction graph, severely compromising both verification efficiency and chain storage capacity. To counterbalance privacy with functionality, the invention introduces "Adaptive RingCT with Delegated Pre-Hashing." This refined protocol streamlines verification logic, expands speed by approximately a factor of ten, and significantly reduces on-chain bloat while preserving core privacy features. Crucially, this model relies entirely on trustless cryptographic verifications, requiring no trust in any participant.

This study examines the relationships among various linear system solvers, such as Kaczmarz, Least Mean Squares, Normal Equations, Momentum, Conjugate Gradient, and the limited-memory Conjugate Gradient. We demonstrate that these connections can be realized as reductions in circuit complexity: the process takes place within a class of circuits characterized by linear switching elements and arithmetic operations of fixed bit-size, where a lower-order solution is solved by directly unrolling the solution upper-hand of a lower-order solution. This approach demonstrates that Kaczmarz, LMS, and Momentum methods Nash equilibriums in terms of computational power, as does the Conjugate Gradient and Limited-Memory Conjugate Gradient. As a result, any algorithm among this group can be reduced to any other in polynomial circuit circuits. As an application, this allows proving that any polynomial time algorithm for a certain type of problem, such as least-squares with polynomial time steps, can be reduced to a least of a certain type.

This study presents the initial, independent measurements of $pp \to WWW$ and $pp \to WZ$ production using 37 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, gathered by the CMS detector at the LHC. Resonances in the system of three or four leptons, respectively, are analyzed to extract cross-sections for these processes. The reported $pp \to WZ$ and $WWZ$ production cross-sections match Standard Model predictions with discrepancies within approximately 2 standard deviations. A detailed analysis of the three-boson system utilizes the matrix-element method to determine the scattering amplitude for $pp \to WWW$. This approach identifies a significant excess at low parton-level invariant masses, yet the resulting tri-boson $pp \to WWW$ production cross-section aligns with theoretical predictions consistent with the Standard Model to an accuracy of roughly 1.5 standard deviations.

This study introduces a new, fully annotated Hebrew UD treebank. It expands the original 2009 Hebrew corpus by 300,000 tokens of newly tagged data from four distinct domains. Utilizing the same Universal Dependencies guidelines as the original corpus but incorporating CoNLL 2012 standards, this updated collection doubles the annotation time and effort. A comprehensive assessment demonstrates that incorporating this enriched corpus has significantly advanced state-of-the-art performance across multiple Hebrew NLP tasks since the 2019 release. Additionally, the research presents a systematic analysis of annotation consistency, quality assurance procedures, and the statistical properties of the enhanced corpus.

When the $p$-adic unit ball, denoted as $B_p$, is viewed as a unit vector space under the $\ell_p$ norm, its linear operators do not generally admit $\epsilon$-isometric reduction for any $\epsilon > 0$ unless the dimensionality parameter $p=2$. This paper demonstrates that such linear mappings lack the required property for any $\epsilon > 0$ where the dimensionality parameter is any other value. However, we show that significant improvements are possible by shifting the reduction focus from linear operators to weakly continuous mappings. Specifically, we prove the existence of a sequence of dimensionality reductions for any $\gamma < 1$ achieved via a weakly continuous transformation that incurs an error of at most $\delta$, provided that the dimensionality parameter is not equal to 2.

Concurrent neural network methods need to be trained on numerous datasets; however, in many real-world scenarios, acquiring sufficient labeled data is difficult. To address this, we introduce a novel method for continual learning of plasticity models in solid mechanics, an approach capable of unifying multiple plasticity models trained on distinct datasets into a single framework. This technique enables the efficient training of robust, generalizable models for simulating solid mechanical behavior, with a specific focus on volume-preserving, history-dependent plasticity. We validate our approach by continuing the training of neural operator models for Olin-Shockley (O-S) and Mroz (M) plasticity models across an extended set comprising the Batdorf-Binkley (B-B), Ilyushin (I), and Razzak (R) models. The results demonstrate that the proposed method produces superior outcomes compared to baseline strategies, generating a compact model with enhanced accuracy in approximating both stress-strain responses and the evolution of yield surfaces under varying loading conditions.

This study introduces a straightforward method to derive a lower bound for the maximum permissible erasure probability ($\epsilon$) in LDPC codes that feature negative degree-correlation among their erasures. This bound is determined by solving a system of linear equations, which can subsequently be enhanced to approach the actual erasure capacity by incorporating the average degree of subgraphs with an odd number of nodes. Empirical results indicate that this proposed bound is remarkably close to the achieved maximum $ \epsilon$ for sparsely connected graphs exhibiting negative correlation. Furthermore, the authors expand their analytical framework by generalizing the bound for cases involving the mean degree of these odd-sized subgraphs. This extension effectively bounds the performance of several well-established ensembles, such as Gallager's B-E and quasi-cycle codes.

This study presents an iterative scheme known as SL-MPSF for computing the matrix exponential of a linear system. Designed to accommodate bounded disturbances, the protocol guarantees safety by maintaining the system within an invariant set. Additionally, it ensures convergence to the true matrix exponential despite disturbances. An SMPSF-based implementation scheme is developed, with its numerical properties rigorously analyzed.

The evolution of practical vacuum and weak decoy-state quantum key distribution (QKD) has led some researchers to theorize that an undetected eavesdropper could launch a specific attack, potentially halting operations while covertly extracting maximal secret key information. This scenario imposes a critical requirement: identifying such an attack demands a full characterization of the QKD source. However, due to limited resources in real-world settings, complete source analysis might be unattainable. This paper proposes an alternative strategy wherein the interceptor acquires the ability to either seize all, the majority of, or a substantial portion of the key material with only a low probability of detection, all the while avoiding the need to pinpoint the attacker's mechanisms. We demonstrate that an entity with access (and a high degree of suspicion) to the QKD systems currently in use could, undetected, seize nearly all the key information through this approach.

Few-shot in-context learning (ICL) has garnered significant interest as a mechanism for deploying pre-trained language models on diverse tasks without extensive fine-tuning. A prevailing hypothesis suggests that low perplexity indicates a model's capacity to capture essential features of the training data, serving as a reliable predictor of downstream task performance. However, this study presents evidence contrary to that assumption, demonstrating that high performance does not always result from low perplexity, particularly in few-shot ICL scenarios. We observe a consistent disconnect between perplexity scores and performance across both natural language processing (NLP) and code tasks. Specifically, the correlation between perplexity and performance weakens substantially as task complexity rises and the amount of provided few-shot samples decreases. These findings suggest that relying on perplexity as a standalone metric for evaluating pre-trained models in the context of few-shot ICL may be flawed.

We investigate the conduction-fueled accretion of cold gas within the intracluster medium (ICM), focusing on how anisotropic thermal conduction influences this process. Building on anisotropy models that align conduction flux with density and temperature gradients, we constructed a one-dimensional, time-dependent hydrodynamical model of a supersonic shock. This model simulates the cooling of shocked gas and the subsequent contraction of an adjacent, pre-cool front, explicitly accounting for the time-varying direction of the conduction heat flux. Our results demonstrate that including anisotropy can elevate the growth rate of the resulting cold gas structures by a factor of two or more compared to isotropic cases. Furthermore, we assessed the sensitivity of these instabilities to the strength of the upstream ICM temperature gradient; while the pre-heating of the shock depends on the gradient, the post-cool front behavior shows greater complexity. In steeper gradient scenarios, the cold gas may either contract steadily or undergo small-scale fragmentation and oscillation before collapsing. These findings underscore that anisotropic thermal conduction can substantially amplify the production of cooling accretion features in galaxy clusters.

This study introduces novel computations of hard scattering string theory. We present explicit evaluations for tree-level 4-point and tree-level 5-point (along with one-loop 4-point) superstring scattering processes involving massive states. These results are expressed in terms of parameters from the Neveu-Schwarz superstring framework and demonstrate invariance under the $SL(5,\mathbb{Z})$ symmetry, consistent with expectations from E$_{5}$. Consequently, these findings suggest that such supersymmetry persists into higher loops and higher mass excitation domains. Furthermore, our results explicitly validate and complete a previous proposal by the same group regarding hard scattering string theory and massive E$_{5}$.

The surging demand for edge computing has intensified the necessity for optimizing operations within edge data centers. This paper introduces three optimization strategies designed to minimize power usage, improve load balancing, and ensure timely task delivery. Specifically, we propose three mathematical formulations addressed via integer linear programming to solve the Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) challenges arising in virtual machine (VM) placement, load balancing, and scheduling. The formulations aim to scale resource allocation and distribute workloads effectively across physical servers (PS) to delay power saturation, simultaneously scheduling tasks to meet performance latency constraints. An experimental assessment utilizing a distributed, stochastic edge environment confirms the approach's validity, demonstrating that our methods successfully reduce energy usage while satisfying operational requirements.

Recent synthesis systems utilizing segmental or frame-level conditional language models have demonstrated significant success. Although these frameworks are highly flexible, the optimal strategy for speech synthesis remains undefined. In this study, we investigate speech synthesis by contrasting two modeling approaches: one that enforces clustering on speech segments and another that regulates the frequency of transient versus steady-state segments. Both methods aim to increase the proportion of steady-state segments to optimize the final output.

We observe that a model governed by transients and steady-states (TSS) achieves superior performance compared to a standard clustering model. Furthermore, we identify a previously unexplored property of steady-states: their optimal count appears determined by both the speech duration and the accumulated clustering cost. Leveraging this insight, we introduce SStTES, a new synthesis framework. Protopostar formation involves collapsing a molecular cloud core, during which an accretion shock forms a flat, rotating disk that evolves into a prolate, rotating structure propped by magnetic fields. While the early accretion phase can eject a substantial amount of mass, the conditions required for this are a subject of debate. This study examines mass ejection in the context of protostar formation using direct numerical simulations of isothermal, magnetized, self-gravitating disks, explicitly including the effects of both cooling and heating. The analysis reveals that shock heating, combined with self-gravity and cooling, drives an unstable radial run-away that results in an unstable, magnetocentrifugal outflow. The resulting outflow rate scales with the surface density of the disk, the specific accretion rate, and the rotation velocity. Notably, the growth of this outflow can become super-exponential, leading to mass loss orders of magnitude greater than the initial accretion rate. Consequently, significant mass loss occurs when a molecular cloud core collapses with a rotation rate exceeding the critical threshold defined by $ \Omega = 0.025 \sqrt{GM/R^3} $. The findings suggest that this mechanism may account for the mass loss and mass ratio asymmetries observed in binary star systems.

To address the safety issues arising from destabilizing variables (DEVs) within nonlinear systems, this paper introduces a novel adaptive fuzzy backstepping sliding mode control (ABSMC) strategy. The methodology begins by constructing a backstepping sliding manifold, followed by the derivation of the specific control law. Design parameters in this ABSMC formula are subsequently tuned using a reinforcement learning (RL) agent via a trial-and-error process. The proposed hybrid ABSRL control scheme effectively mitigates safety threats caused by DEVs by compensating for their adverse impacts through learned optimal control actions. Validation through a case study on an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) confirms the efficacy of this new strategy.

This work examines how Ephemeral Radiation Pressure (YORP) alters the eccentricity and inclination of an unmanned body orbiting the Sun, subject to the constraint that its inclination remains below 45°. The study concentrates on the i:1 and 2:1 orbital resonances between the body's spin period and its orbital period, which amplify the effects of YORP. The analysis delineates the conditions governing the co-evolution of these orbital and rotational periods and evaluates the resulting changes in semi-major axis, eccentricity, and inclination. The variations in eccentricity and inclination depend primarily on the body's equatorial radius, its moment of inertia, and its rotational velocity. The research outlines the i:1 and 2:1 resonance types, noting that YORP-induced amplitude in the i:1 resonance is 1.5 to 2 times greater than in the 2:1 resonance. The i:1 resonance, which occurs at larger orbital distances, generates inclinations up to 1.5° for objects larger than 200 m, whereas inclinations in the 2:1 resonance are less than 0.5° regardless of size. For bodies exceeding 200 m in the i:1 resonance, inclinations can surpass 0.5°; however, inclinations in the 2:1 resonance remain below 0.5° for all bodies. The paper also evaluates the timescales required for these resonant effects

The velocity gauge within tight-binding models presents significant drawbacks when modeling electromagnetic responses in the presence of vector potentials, specifically due to the absence of a length scale, which often results in physically meaningless numerical outcomes. To overcome this, we introduce a weak-dispersion k\cdot\text{-p} based tight-binding framework formulated in the position gauge. This model is constructed in slabs of finite thickness and effectively addresses infinite systems by eliminating surface artifacts through the application of complex surface masses. Despite its relative complexity, this framework is viable for numerical implementation. We validate its utility by analyzing the magnetic response of artificially corrugated TIs and modeling the anomalous Hall effect in systems lacking inversion symmetry, demonstrating that it outperforms the momentum-space velocity gauge and the standard real-space vector-inclusion method in precision, all while maintaining reasonable computational efficiency.

By leveraging the geometric properties of the 3D Hough Transform, transform errors into weights that serve as measures of similarity within a weighted graph representing the 3D Hough feature space. The proposed "link-based" strategy is more resilient to noise than traditional "distance-based" calculations. For partitioning this weighted graph into coherent clusters, we employ state-of-the-art max-flow/min-cut algorithms. The effectiveness of our "weight-as-outlier-estimate" framework combined with graph-cut segmentation is demonstrated through experiments, which highlight its superior performance in achieving robust pose and shape estimation.

Borrowing information across subgroups has gained popularity in clinical trials to enhance the efficiency of treatment parameter estimation. While most current methods apply to homogeneous treatment effects or effects that vary only by site characteristics, emerging techniques now accommodate more complex, heterogenous responses. This study presents a multiple imputation approach designed to borrow data from commutative subgroups and demonstrates its effectiveness through a simulation framework. The equivalent sample size within shared groups highlights how the methodology reduces trial requirements while managing heterogeneity.

This study addresses the synchronization problem for a class of lower triangular systems affected by internal states and external disturbances. Specifically, position-dependent dynamics, which hinder decoupling-based design, are incorporated. An adaptive nonlinear proportional-integral (PI) sliding mode controller is proposed to achieve adaptive backlash compensation and simultaneously ensure exponential convergence of the synchronization error. These convergence properties are verified using a Lyapunov function and the LaSalle Invariance Principle. Finally, simulation results involving robot arm tracking and a two-wheeled self-balancing robot demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed control strategy.

We introduce a deep-learning-based registration system designed for single-pair point cloud alignment that generates representations beneficial for downstream tasks. This approach models registration as a regression problem, leveraging learned features to effectively classify the dominant transformation type and refine the registration through iterative optimization. Evaluation across the 4Part benchmark and the NYUV40 dataset demonstrates that the network accurately predicts transformation categories and enhances registration precision via iterative refinement. Furthermore, utilizing learned features for classification achieves state-of-the-art results on 4Part, and these features show strong potential for standard classification when combined with 4Part-specific category labels.

A proposed proposal outlines a strategy for determining the top quark mass at future low-energy colliders, such as those featuring a small e+e- machine or muon collider prototype. This plan involves a comprehensive, self-contained measurement of the t\bar{t} threshold scan and the analysis of hadronic top decay. The required energy range, spanning from 350 GeV to 1 TeV, is attainable on an NLC-type muon collider or, alternatively, as part of an ILC-type linear accelerator. The text describes the concept of the "Mu3e" project, which aims to achieve an unprecedented sensitivity of 10$^{-21}$ in lepton flavor universality tests by employing low background, high-luminosity techniques to detect rare muon decays mediated by weak interactions. The required sensitivity for this process can likely be achieved using a dedicated detector designed for muon colliders, which would also provide the necessary instrumentation and capabilities for accurately resolving the top quark mass.

Quantum chemistry has seen a significant breakthrough with the advent of ab initio methods capable of handling many-body dynamics over ultrafast timescales. However, integrating these methods with experiment presents a hurdle, primarily due to the low signal-to-noise ratio found in ultrafast laboratory data, which complicates traditional inversion techniques. This study introduces a novel inversion approach designed to effectively handle noise while addressing the ill-posed nature of the problem through regularization. The specific form of the regularization is determined using the Losilla-Marrero-Goldstein-Louis (LMR) criterion, while the corresponding parameters are optimized via the Unsupervised Learning (UL) or Losilla-Langford-Langford-Louis (LL) algorithm, offering a robust framework for HHI analysis. To demonstrate its efficacy, the method was applied to HHI data, revealing a precise determination of both optimal regularization parameters and electronic parameters, with results showing a near-perfect alignment between simulated and experimental outcomes.

This study calculates light-cone distribution amplitudes (LCDAs) for $\rho$, $\rho^*$, and $D^*_s$ mesons within the framework of QCD, employing the method of perturbative QCD. We adopt a Fock space representation to derive both leading-order (LO) and next-to-leading-order (NLO) contributions to LO mixing coefficients, ultimately determining LO and NLO values for the total mixing parameters. Our results indicate that the $\rho$ and $\rho^*$ mesons maintain approximate $u-d$ quark flavor symmetry with NLO enhancements around 20%, whereas significant mass disparity between the charm and strange quarks causes NLO mixing coefficients to dominate in the $D^*_s$ meson. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the momentum distributions among quarks within these mesons closely resemble those found in pseudoscalar mesons.

This article examines the connection between a function's asymptotic growth estimates and its corresponding Fourier transform within the framework of Gelfand-Shilov spaces. The study derives novel inequalities for ultradifferentiable functions, defined by a convexity condition on the weight sequence $[\lambda_m]$, specifically targeting those generated by a convex function $\omega(m)$. These results extend and enhance the classical uncertainty principle, with applications particularly noted in the context of the Hermite transform.

A significant hurdle in medical instance segmentation is the scarcity of sufficiently large, expert-annotated datasets. While recent segmentation frameworks have improved performance on abundant labeled data, they often remain constrained by such dataset size limitations. To address this, we introduce CySGAN, a novel generative adversarial network designed to reduce dependency on extensive annotation sets. Our method functions by creating expert-driven synthetic annotations for unlabeled data through a segmentation model trained on a small initial training cohort. These synthesized labels subsequently expand the training data, effectively minimizing the need for manual expert labeling. We evaluated CyGAN on the challenging task of segmenting cysts within retinal fundus images, utilizing a minimal Small Object Segmentation (SOS) dataset. Our results indicate that CyGAN enhances segmentation accuracy on both seen and unseen test sets, surpassing State-of-the-Art models trained exclusively on small data. Additionally, the approach successfully cuts annotation expenses by 90% without sacrificing, and often improving, performance. Source code is accessible at https://github.com/retinamicro/AI/tree/main/CyGAN.

Deep learning has achieved significant success in the challenge of action prediction, yet current models frequently depend on manual feature engineering. This paper introduces an innovative solution utilizing Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernels to refine this process. By effectively modeling feature space, this approach facilitates more efficient learning and subsequently enhances prediction performance. Experimental evaluations confirm that utilizing RBF kernels with appropriate centers and variance yields superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art methods on two major benchmarks: UTD-MotionCapitation and UTD-MotionUtilization.

Specifically, the broadening of hydrogen lines is driven by continuum-driven convective motions, with our findings showing that surface velocities during flares are significantly higher than in standard quiescent phases. This paper introduces a new framework for training robust TCP (Twisting, Compositionality, and Proximity) point cloud models, specifically designed to enable certified defense against twisting transformations. We present a deterministic protocol to verify robustness by generating adversarial twist angles that guarantee specific model performance thresholds. Leveraging this method, the study develops an effective training approach to establish lower bounds for accuracy across these worst-case scenarios, thereby providing formal robustness certificates for various model sizes. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our certificates significantly exceed those of prior methods in area and effectiveness while simultaneously improving worst-case accuracy by approximately 10-15 percentage points across different scaled models, all without incurring additional computational overhead.

It treats the free fermions as infinitely many individual fermions, each governed by a Grassmann-odd scalar field, and presents a degree-counting argument that establishes the equivalence between this field and a field with odd bosonic character.

We introduce Cycene, a novel attention-based model for completing temporal knowledge graphs that integrates cycle-aware time encoding with an attention mechanism for interactions. Specifically, Cycene employs an attention mechanism to couple temporal encodings with cycle-aware schemes, effectively handling the irregular spacing and variability in timing between different triples. Empirical results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art models. Notably, Cycene achieves superior performance on the 1M Movie Triads dataset, a dataset characterized by high sparsity and complexity, confirming the effectiveness of its unique architecture.

This study investigates the conditions under which ground noise becomes audible in the near-field, specifically focusing on impact sounds generated in a half-space. We present an approximation of the impulsive Green's function Green's function for a point source in a half-space, allowing for accurate near-field calculations of Green's function for a point source in a half-space. This enables precise near-field evaluations of the impulse response for various materials, including concrete, aluminum, wood, and soil. Consequently, we can determine the audible frequency bands for impacts occurring on these surfaces. Our analysis indicates that ground noise in these scenarios is audible only over a restricted range of frequencies and at very close proximities. We also compare our results against finite element method (FEM) simulations, which confirm that the proposed analytical model is accurate enough for practical use.

Recent research has established that measurement-device-independent (MDI) quantum protocols, while not eliminating Bell inequalities perfectly, do not incur the full associated cost. In this study, we examine how these residual correlations impact various aspects of Bell nonlocality and measurement nonlocality within the context of quantum information. Our analysis indicates that while the fundamental definitions and formal structures of nonlocality remain unchanged, the quantitative characteristics—particularly regarding quantum nonlocality—are significantly altered. Specifically, we evaluate changes within the Tsirelson bound, quantum nonlocality volume, quantum nonlocality area, quantum nonlocality radius, quantum nonlocality entropy, and quantum nonlocality distance. Our findings demonstrate that the upper limits for Tsirelson bounds are raised by noise. Furthermore, by proposing a new concept termed the "quantum nonlocality diameter," we assess these modifications to understand their implications for quantum information processing technologies and applications.

This study reexamines the degeneracy of flat-band systems characterized by a mean degeneracy of $D$. It demonstrates that introducing randomness within a tight-binding framework, specifically affecting a single term out of $D$ equivalent orbitals per molecule, typically breaks the flat band. However, a degenerate subset of states can persist under specific conditions, with their count determined largely by the intrinsic degeneracy $D$ rather than the strength of the perturbing random element. Numerical simulations indicate that for systems where $D=2$ or $D=3$, a robust flat band remains stable even with considerable disorder. Furthermore, these simulations suggest that $D=2$ and $D=3$ flat bands exhibit a power-law distribution for their energies relative to the band bottom, whereas $D=1$ and $B=10$ (note: likely a typo in original for "or $D=10$") distributions follow an exponential decay.

The electron-phonon coupling in hydrogen borane (HBB) monolayers, a recently identified two-dimensional superconductor, is examined using *ab initio* calculations. Monolayers composed of vertical H-B-B chains exhibit distinct phonon dispersion, with the H-B-B vibrational modes showing strong coupling to the superconducting gap. First, we find that including hydrogen atoms significantly alters electron-phonon interactions. Specifically, at low doping levels, superconductivity is driven by vibrations of the hydrogen-bearing bond, whereas high doping shifts the dominant coupling to B-B bond vibrations. Additionally, isotopic substitution of hydrogen alters both the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) and doping-dependent phonon characteristics, underscoring the critical role of the hydrogen atom in the mechanism of superconductivity within this material.

This paper examines the behavior of measure-class-preserving actions of actions on the space of homomorphisms into ${{\mathbb R}}^n$, known as character spaces, which occur in finitely generated nilpotent groups. The work demonstrates that the dynamic behavior of these actions mirrors the well-understood dynamics on torus character spaces. The primary technique employed is the utilization of Milnor-Shishikura invariants.

Formal verification methods, including model checking, have emerged as essential tools for the early detection and correction of flaws in automotive driving systems. This study extends the model-checking approach to handle more complex, full-scale automotive software architectures, specifically those utilizing high-level block diagrams. By employing an iterative refinement technique, intermediate versions of the software are verified; this process allows errors in both low-level implementations and the interfaces between components to be identified and fixed. This verification loop continues until the final version is verified with a conformance level matching the original specification's intended safety standard. To achieve this, the methodology integrates model checking with execution tracing and utilizes a binary encoding format to distinguish verified blocks from unverified ones. This separation enables the model checker to confirm safe operation within verified sections while simultaneously tracing the execution of the system, including unverified sections, to the conclusion.

The Koopman operator framework offers a potent approach to analyzing and controlling nonlinear dynamical systems by linearizing them through elevation to subspaces of observable functions. Evidence suggests that finite-dimensional approximations of this operator can effectively reveal coherent structures in state spaces and optimize control strategies. Notably, as the system dimension increases, so too does the computational difficulty; however, this challenge can be met with the deployment of tensor products. In this context we introduce a novel representation of the Koopman operator constructed via the cross tensor of observable functions, and a corresponding update algorithm suited for gradient-based analysis and optimization.

This paper examines Leibniz's inferences regarding the concepts of the bounded and the unbounded, as well as infinite divisibility, drawn from his correspondence with Arnauld and his *New Essays*. It argues against the view held by scholars such as Bell, Koyré, and Pannekoek—that the 17th century saw a continuity in thinking regarding the bounded versus the unlimited—by suggesting instead a persistent shift in Leibniz's thought. Specifically, one can observe a movement from his initial alignment with the "bounded" tradition toward a later preference for "unlimited" thinking. We contend that even in his mature years, as suggested by passages in the *New Essays*, there remains ambiguity regarding what exactly Leibniz intended to convey.

We evaluate the influences of foreground subtraction schemes on cosmological parameter constraints derived from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) 3GHz survey. Utilizing a power spectrum-based cleaning method alongside a suite of full-sky simulations, we quantify the resulting biases and uncertainties on the angular power spectrum, the CMB blackbody properties, and key cosmological parameters. Our results indicate that while foreground cleaning introduces negligible bias to the CMB temperature spectrum, it induces a slight shift in the spectrum's shape that peaks near 1000 degrees, resulting in a change to the amplitude of the $C_\ell$ spectrum of at most 0.1\%. These effects are even smaller when the spectrum is binned for standard cosmological inference, altering the final parameter estimates by less than 0.05%.

Let $\{x_n\}$ be a sequence of nonzero vectors and $T$ be a linear operator such that $\{Tx_n\}$ is also sequence of nonzero vectors. If $\{Tx_n\}$ remains linearly independent every time $\{x_n\}$ is linearly independent, we say $T$ is a map-preserving operator (Tmpo). When $\{Tx_n\}$ is minimal whenever $\{x_n\}$ is minimal, $T$ is called a minimality mapping operator (Mmmo). This paper demonstrates the equivalence between an operator being an Mmmo and being a Tmpo under the condition that both possess a common common sequence $\{x_n\}$ of nonzero vectors that is either linearly independent or merely minimal.

Traditional user-item collaborative filtering (CF) techniques falter under data sparsity, prompting the development of alternative approaches like content-based CF and hybrid models. In contrast, this study introduces a novel, hybridized, latent factor model that leverages document modeling. This approach treats individual items as documents, constructs a term-item matrix where terms represent other items, and utilizes pre-trained term vectors (such as those from Word2Vec) to substitute missing entries. By integrating side information and normalizing item interactions, the proposed method addresses user sparsity effectively. Empirical evaluations on two large-scale industrial datasets confirm that this technique surpasses existing state-of-the-art systems in recommendation accuracy.

Conditional freeness serves as an extension of the concept of freeness from probability, acting as a robust instrument in analyzing the eigenvalues associated with the sum and product of deterministic functions of symmetric block matrices. The paper by the authors introduces a novel methodology to establish the conditional freeness of specific polynomial functions of these matrices, leveraging this result to derive the eigenvalue concentration for their normalized sum and product. The demonstration relies fundamentally on the property of semi-circular decomposition and the application of the Dyson equation.

Model checking serves as a prevalent strategy for supervising the execution of distributed programs. To handle timing uncertainties, some approaches monitor based on the elapsed real wall-clock time, while others base decisions on the alternative number of computational steps. This work introduces and analyzes the concept of "adaptive model checking," a technique that dynamically selects between validation based on step count or actual time to optimize performance. The primary goal is to minimize the average duration required for monitoring while ensuring correctness. This average is calculated as a weighted sum of system activity duration and the variance in both the monitored steps taken and the elapsed time. Assuming a Markovian behavior for the underlying program, the problem can be formulated as a linear programming problem to compute an optimal policy. The resulting strategy leverages context-aware dynamic selection between time-based and step-based model checking, effectively balancing monitoring efficiency and correctness.

This document details the calibration process of the GRAVITY instrument at the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI), which relies on four 16-metre baselines. It describes a "quick-look" mode operating via on-board processing, utilizing data from an acquisition camera to automatically stabilize both the active and passive optical paths. These stabilization parameters, generated in this mode, are then employed during the primary observations to facilitate efficient operation and ensure that full-quality measurements can be executed in any good observing conditions.

The Capacitated $k$-Center problem, often abbreviated as the CkC problem, involves selecting exactly $k$ facilities to optimize a solution where clients, each with specific demand, must be assigned to these centers. A critical constraint requires that no facility serves more than its designated capacity, necessitating that clients with demands exceeding this limit be grouped accordingly. Historically, given the strong lower bounds indicating CkC is harder to approximate than Capacitated $\epsilon$-Centers with Outliers (C$\epsilon$Co)—even when analyzing instances with a fixed, small highway dimension—it was assumed the former resisted similar approximation ratios. In this work, however, we demonstrate that for C$\epsilon$Co instances constrained by low highway dimension, a constant-factor constant-factor approximation is achievable using only polynomial time, a finding that indirectly proves significant approximability for the CkC problem. To reach these bounds, we present an algorithm rooted in a new density lemma. This lemma establishes that for both CkC and C$\epsilon$Co instances, a collection of well-dense subsets exists; within these subsets, every point maintains proximity to a dense cluster, defined such that the count of points within a bounded distance is limited. Crucially, this technique yields a constant factor for C$\epsilon$Co by ensuring the subsets are sufficiently sparse. Building on this foundation, we introduce a recursive partitioning strategy that breaks large dense clusters into smaller ones, solving the problem iteratively.

This paper begins by resolving the Brück conjecture specifically for the equation $e^z f^n + P(e^z)f + Q(e^z) = 1$, where $f$ is an entire function whose hyper-order is less than 1/1.1. Additionally, a Brück-type result is established under the assumption that $f$ is a meromorphic finite-type meromorphic function and $P$ and $Q$ are polynomials such that $f$ omits no values in $\mathbb{C}$. Finally, the author presents several examples to demonstrate the optimality of the constraints imposed in the main theorems.

The current research enhances the Calvetti-Reichel approach by limiting the required polynomial evaluations and demonstrating how to incorporate a tolerance level for inaccuracies in the inverse matrix.

The study introduces a new equation of state for the high-pressure compressibility of alkali metals, grounded in their dynamic electronic structure under extreme pressure. This model adheres to the principle of corresponding states and derives a universal functional form for the inverse bulk modulus that relies solely on a specific set of reduced variables: relative pressure, relative volume, and a characteristic electronic parameter. High-computational accuracy in predicting high-pressure compressibility for lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, and cesium—achieved via density functional theory (DFT) with the PBE functional—validates this universal formula. The approach successfully maps the alkali-specific DFT data onto a single curve, with minor deviations (<2%) attributed to high-$k$ electronic structure nuances. These findings suggest the universal equation can be extended to other elemental groups once a suitable mapping strategy is identified. Furthermore, the study calculates high-pressure melting points for the same alkali series using a simplified weak-coupling Landau theory, revealing a dependence on electron count and demonstrating a power-law relationship with melting temperature as a function of zero-pressure volume.

We examine the formation of vector mesons within a parity-violating environment that includes the Chern-Simons term by solving the Bethe-Salpeter equation. Our results indicate that while the vacuum exhibits spin polarization of the generated mesons, the local parity breaking of the medium induces both a shift in the meson's mass and a variation in the magnitude of its spin polarization. Furthermore, we observe a dependence of these spin polarization and mass values on the meson's orientation relative to the magnetic field, as well as their dependence on the magnitude of the Chern-Simons term itself.

This paper introduces a randomized distributed algorithm designed for estimating the volume of distributed networks, specifically targeting sparsely connected graphs. The approach is both simple and highly effective, maintaining an approximately uniform distribution of sampling nodes throughout the network. It operates within an asymmetric environment using only $O(\log n)$ memory per node and converges in $O(\log n)$ rounds in expectation. The algorithm's performance relies on the Strongly Connected Component (SCC) framework in its proof of correctness. Furthermore, the demonstration of its correctness and the derivation of the associated bounds leverage both traditional and novel techniques drawn from percolation theory.

A novel scheme for solving the Hamiltonian constraint is introduced, described as "semi-conformal" because it solves the conformally related regularized constraint numerically while allowing conformal factors to be determined with multiple levels of refinement. This approach is both fully adaptive and fully conservative. Its derivation stems from the time-convex formulation of the constraint; solving this form yields both the necessary information and the pre-image conformal factor. Note that this is not "1D post-processing," as solving in higher dimensions is required to determine this pre-mapped factor. Instead, the method operates by solving in a single high-dimensional post-conformal framework. What emerges is a robust, stable solution to the constraint that remains independent of the specific choices made regarding conformal factor decomposition or the corresponding variables.

The LAZIX project, a detector prototype for JUNO (a next-generation neutrino observation experiment at China's Yangyang), is designed with approximately 400 tons of ultra-pure water serving both as the target and scintillation medium, instrumented with 1,350 highly sensitive, fast 5-inch photomultiplier tubes. This paper outlines current progress in simlazation, single photon reconstruction, and the identification of neutrino-related events using JUNO-like simulator.

This paper introduces an enhanced Informer model designed for predicting Multivariate Time Series (MTS). The model improves upon the original架构 by cross-modifying cross-attention mechanisms to strengthen relationships across dimensions, utilizing a multi-head setup to focus on long-term temporal patterns, and integrating a hybrid loss function to address varying scales. Evaluated on the AutoSet benchmark, the proposed "NewInformer" surpasses leading baselines, achieving reductions of 10.3% to 30.3% in Root Mean Square Error.

This study evaluates the performance of the Blue Albedo Detector (BAD) within the Greenhouse Atmosphere Biosphere Physics Experiment (GABRIEL) mission, which aims to detect water vapor and oxygen in Venus's atmosphere. The mission will deploy a radiofrequency sounder to Venus's surface, collecting data across a frequency range of 490 to 580 MHz. The analysis compares two atmospheric models: the standard spherically symmetric approach and the Azimuth-Range-Azimuth (ARA) scheme, the latter tailored for dispersion characteristics in the radio frequency domain. The research contrasts these methods by simulating the radio frequency signals at the Venus's surface across a frequency range of 490 to 580 MHz. In classification tasks, utilizing both pairwise relationships between samples and their label information can enhance performance. While prior methods leveraging sample relations often depend on discrete labels for constraints or loss calculation, we introduce a novel approach that extracts these pairwise connections in an unsupervised manner. Fundamentally based on logit ensemble techniques, our Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) algorithm engages in successive iterations to aggregate relabel samples relative to others during training. Crucially, given the iterative nature of many popular ensemble strategies, PPILE effectively integrates pair-wise sample dynamics into standard ensemble ensembling. Evaluations across multiple object detection and classification benchmarks demonstrate that PPILE outperforms prior pair-wise methods as well as conventional supervised and unsupervised alternatives, achieving superior accuracy with minimal computational overhead.

Ultralight bosonic dark matter interacting with standard model particles may induce fleeting stochastic intensity variations in the nuclear recoil rate within a single detector. Uncovering such a signal is significantly more feasible using a coordinated network of sensors, as the capability to identify these fluctuations scales with the total exposed mass across the entire network. We introduce a detection framework based on principal component analysis, which allows for constraints on ultralight bosonic dark matter in the $10^{-8}$ eV to $10^{-5}$ eV mass range by searching for these intensity modulations. Our approach enlarges single-device search volumes by an order of magnitude or greater in scenarios where the recoil rate exhibits weak time correlation, and we rigorously assess the significant impact of the "common-mode" assumption on result reliability.

This paper investigates how the spectrum of a measurement matrix $A$ impacts the likelihood of finding sparse solutions in basis pursuit. The study reveals a strong correlation: when the spectrum of $A$ concentrates a specific number of eigenvalues near unit modulus, and the noise vector $\delta$ has significant components in those corresponding eigenspaces, finding a sparse solution becomes increasingly improbable. Furthermore, these findings are validated through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.

Recent advances in programmable network-in-the-loop (PiLo) research have enabled the rapid development of new theories, algorithms, and protocols. However, the field is constrained by a scarcity of publicly available, open-source TTP4242 (P4-14/TTP4244) compiler backends, which hinders the verification and comparison of these innovations. To address this limitation, this paper introduces P4PiLo, a dedicated P4PiLo simulator that functions as a lightweight, single-threaded software model. It provides essential support for designing various PiLo experiments, including the validation and comparison of such developments. The study validates the simulator by porting and running three existing algorithms, finding that its results align with those produced by larger existing simulators. Additionally, the authors showcase the utilization of P4PiLo in the design, implementation, and execution of a new TTP4244 based P4PiLo algorithm for a specific use case.

This study introduces a mixed finite element formulation of the vector transport equation that explicitly accommodates both a vector field and a scalar pressure field as solutions. By applying a Lagrange multiplier method, the angular metric of the rotation is utilized to ensure exact and constraint-based admissibility of the computed translational pressure. Solving the resulting system with a Newton-Krylov algorithm demonstrates that this approach significantly improves transport accuracy by capturing recirculation zones and avoiding spurious modes, findings which are validated through the vector Advection-Rotational-Magneto-Diffusion (ARDM) test case.

Machine learning (ML) has significantly transformed our daily lives, yet its deployment frequently raises moral and social concerns. To mitigate these issues, three primary approaches have emerged: federated learning (FL), differential privacy (DP), and fairness metrics. While FL tackles ethical concerns regarding user data privacy, DP offers guarantees at the theoretical level, and fairness metrics provide ways to ensure equitable model outcomes. In this study, we analytically determine the fair-privacy loss incurred in a differential privacy setting applied to a federated model. Specifically, this work offers a formal demonstration that standard FL is incompatible with most common utility fairness metrics unless no privacy noise is added to gradient updates. Conversely, when noise proportional to the Fisher information matrix is introduced during updates, the resulting model satisfies these fairness metrics. To our knowledge, this represents the first proof establishing a connection among utility fairness, federated learning, and differential privacy.

This study examines the $pp$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, utilizing a dataset with an integrated luminosity of $65.4\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ to search for $B_c^+(X) \to J/\psi(K_S^0)$ decays. Analysis of the invariant-mass spectrum of $B_c^+(X) \to J/\psi(K_S^0)$ reveals two distinct peaks, identifying the $B_c^+(1n)$ and $B_c^+(2j)$ excited states. The observed yields for $B_c^+(1n)$ and $B_c^+(2j)$ are $102.4 \pm 1.8 (stat) \pm 6.4 (stat)$ and $102.4 \pm 1.8 (stat) \pm 6.4 (stat)$ respectively, with no significant evidence for other $B_c^+(X)$ contributions.

This study investigates a class of linear, time-dependent Hamiltonian systems. We analyze the relationship between continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods and a specific Hamiltonian structure. It is demonstrated that continuous-run Runge-Kutta schemes of any order $\ge 3$ can interpret as a symplectic linear multistatic method with polynomial continuity conditions. We establish an explicit, algebraic, and sufficient condition linking the butts of the continuous-stage Runge-Kutta method and the polynomial continuity conditions to ensure that these methods act as symmetery Hamiltonian schemes. We then consider how to enhance efficiency by minimizing the number of non-zero matrix entries in the coefficient structures associated with continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods of the Hamiltonian schemes. Finally, we provide an explicit, closed-form solution for determining the continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods and continuity conditions that satisfy the required conditions for any given order.

Convolutional and recurrent neural networks are typically trained using backpropagation through time, a method characterized by its significant memory consumption and computational demands. This paper introduces an unsupervised pre-training strategy designed to enhance the efficiency of these architectures by employing a "local critic" that approximates the derivatives of a global critic. The work demonstrates the application of these methods within recurrent neural networks and convolutive autoencoders, successfully reducing both the memory footprint and training time while maintaining model performance equivalent to standard deep learning benchmarks.

This study examines how minor dissipative effects alter chaotic scattering involving three rotating disks. The dynamics, which are conservative when all disks share identical radii in the Hamiltonian framework, were simulated using the Flexible Wing Microrobot (FWM) model. Results indicate that even slight energy loss stabilizes Wada basins, causing them to expand by orders of magnitude in size. This expansion makes a significantly larger portion of the initial phase space chaotic, thereby drastically increasing complexity. The largest Wada basin observed in this dissipative scenario covers approximately 27.6% of the total phase space. Furthermore, the fractal dimension of the Wada islands rises nearly to the dimension of the phase space itself as the energy dissipation coefficient increases. The article concludes by outlining future avenues for investigation within this field.

To probe the muon g-2 anomaly, the paper introduces a low-energy dark photon model featuring kinetic mixing, alongside a detailed analysis of a potential SHiP experiment at CERN. The authors examine how SHiP can explore under-investigated regions of the model's parameter space, specifically through electron-positron collisions, the decay of beams and hadrons, and neutral current processes. A complete framework for a g-2/fixed-target study is presented, which is expected to investigate a significant and previously unexplored section of the relevant parameter space.

Human videos consist of sequences of images where key areas often span across the temporal dimension. Addressing this, we introduce HAN (Hierarchical Attention Network), a deep learning model designed for human keypoint understanding. HAN employs a multi-stage spatial-temporal attention mechanism to identify significant regions within consecutive frames, which it aggregates hierarchically to refine the aggregation through time. This architecture allows HAN to function effectively as a general architecture applicable to various tasks, including in-air exercise classification and analysis of human interactions. Furthermore, HAN proves especially well-suited for domain adaptation; we demonstrate this capability by creating a classifier for in-air exercises, leveraging its strong transfer performance.

We examine collisions of low-energy scalars with an accelerating pair of particles, a setup that simulates the backreaction-free modeling of wave scattering off near-extremal ($q<1$) and extremal ($q=1$) black holes. By allowing the particles to accelerate from rest within a finite region, our analysis reveals a critical distinction between the two scenarios: while the resulting spacetime for a near-extremal hole settles into a stationary black hole, the extremal hole's evolution leads to a final state that is stationary yet horizonless. Furthermore, for a $q<1$ hole, both energy and charge radiated to asymptotic infinity are proportional to $(1-q)$ to the first order.

Star formation is a critical area of research for unraveling the cosmic origins of the elements essential to life on Earth. This study investigates the co-evolution of stars and supermassive black holes within the Milky Way, focusing on a newly identified, compact star-forming cluster in the Galactic Center. Located approximately 2.5 light-years from the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*, this group of about 200 stars—comprising roughly 50 low-mass members—is distinguished by its unusual high density. The authors propose that such an assembly likely arose from the collapse of a giant molecular cloud fragment situated in close proximity to the black hole. By applying a newly developed mathematical model for star formation in strong gravitational fields, we suggest this cluster resulted within approximately 1.5 million years. Furthermore, we provide evidence that the same extreme environment also hosted the growth of Sagittarius A* during this same brief interval.

Determining the entropy of a continuous probability distribution is a common task in fields like machine learning and graphics. However, this task becomes intractable when the distribution cannot be directly evaluated or its derivatives obtained, as is often the case with samples generated via Markov chains or those derived from the ratio of two functions. Although some recent studies have addressed this limitation using approximate Bayesian computation, their proposed estimators remain biased. This paper introduces a fully unbiased method for Monte Carlo estimation of entropy in such constrained settings. The validity of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on high-dimensional distributions, where the resulting estimators exhibit low variance. Consequently, this method is ideally suited for applications such as the model comparison in approximate Bayesian computation and variants of Monte Carlo integration that rely on unbiased algorithms.

This paper applies Borel measures to examine several aspects of infinite-state Markov chains representing complex, finite-dimensional Markov queues with product-form stationary distributions—specifically those conforming to the Grossman, Harchol-Balter, and Harchol frameworks. Measures are utilized first to express state probabilities and current fluxes as well as to derive various performance indices for heavily loaded systems. Furthermore, these tools offer a unifying theoretical framework that explains the structural properties of Grossman's and Harchol's formulas and distinguishes the approaches of these authors from one another.

Coded, a newly developed tool, implements the the NB encoded, allowing for efficient execution of Naive Bayes-based attack classifiers even on resource-constrained devices. It compiles these models into compact, portable functions that operate within a variety of embedded environments by leveraging data types and operations native to the target CPU and memory architecture. This compilation process utilizes a combination of static and dynamic analysis alongside a hand-crafted, custom compiler to convert a standardized, intermediate representation of a classifier into optimized code. The resulting functions maintain logical equivalence to the original algorithm while delivering substantial performance gains, specifically reducing function body size by 90% and lowering inference latency by 30% to 400%. These compact dynamic libraries can be embedded directly within security applications, delivering near real-time accuracy for identifying malicious traffic on a broad spectrum of hardware platforms, ranging from general-purpose processors to microcontrollers.

It is well established that biological and non-biological objects often exhibit distinct movement patterns. This observation has inspired the development of "life detection" systems, which typically rely on statistical analysis of trajectory data to identify signs of biological activity. This paper proposes an alternative "life discrimination" framework grounded in the topological analysis of spatial patterns. We demonstrate through statistical testing that the statistical robustness required to validate our method exceeds the threshold prescribed by the Benferroni-Dunn criterion.

Power networks face growing strain from rising electricity demand and the integration of intermittent renewable energy sources. To alleviate network congestion, solutions must be identified that are both efficient and capable of large-scale deployment. While recent research indicates that quantum algorithms can solve network partitioning problems more quickly than classical algorithms, current quantum hardware remains too small for practical, real-world application. This paper addresses this hardware limitation by introducing a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm designed to tackle these network issues effectively. The study evaluates the performance of this proposed hybrid method against leading hybrid and purely classical benchmarks. Results demonstrate that, compared to existing alternatives, this new hybrid quantum algorithm solves partitioning problems significantly faster.

This study presents a statistical framework to analyze the complexities inherent in estimating the parameters of a falling object model, addressing both measurement noise in position data and the non-stationary nature of fluid drag forces. Adopting a Bayesian approach, we develop a moving least squares scheme that accounts for the uneven vertical acceleration caused by time-dependent drag and noise. Additionally, we quantify the sensitivity of the estimated parameters to these uncertainties by calculating their Bayesian error bars within this non-station context. Validation through both numerical simulations and experimental results involving steel balls dropped in water confirms the proposed model's accuracy and precision.

We investigate a supersymmetry scenario characterized by "stealth" charginos and neutralinos, distinguished by the absence of direct coupling to the Higgs boson. In this setup, the lightest chargino and neutralino masses span from 100 GeV to 3 TeV, ensuring they are produced in pairs via ZZ or WW fusion mechanisms. Current searches at the LHC, which target the decay of the heaviest boson into bosons, have already placed constraints on the signal region covering benchmark Model A up to an integrated luminosity of 35 fb$^{-1}$. Furthermore, we analyze specific supersymmetry benchmark scenarios within this framework, assessing how existing LHC data limits the parameter space for these Higgs-coupling-suppressed states.

We present a model for optimizing the tuning parameters of a taper-based waveguide chip-scale photonic crystal fiber source. This source is intended for quantum information applications and is designed for efficient coupling with single-photon detectors. The proposed configuration includes a reflective section for coupling with an optical fiber, followed by a tapered waveguide that is, in turn, connected to a photonic crystal fiber. The connection point between the single-photon source wave and the taper is critical for optimizing the coupling efficiency. We have determined the optimal parameters for this model using both analytical methods and numerical analysis. Our study examines the relationship between the taper geometry and the resulting transmission spectrum, as well as the characteristics of the photonic crystal fiber's mode field. The resulting numerical spectrum features a prominent transmission peak, with a full-width at half-maximum of 2.5 µm. The model predicts a maximum transmission of 96.5% when the optical fiber has a diameter of 2.45 µm, positioned 20.5 µm from the waveguide. The corresponding taper half-diameter at this location measures 0.35 µm, with the taper tip diameter measuring 0.1 µm. The authors of this paper are the following researchers: M. A. A. A. A. A. A. A. Raman spectroscopy findings concerning the longitudinal sound wave damping in Heisenberg ferromagnets, specifically at low frequencies and high temperatures, align closely with the predictions of the soft potential model. Specifically, the $^3$He soft spin state is a key factor in this phenomenon. The resulting logarithmic dependence on the wave vector, $D(q) \propto q^2\ln(1/q)$, is derived directly from the spectral characteristics of 3D soft spins. Additionally, the magnitude of the linear coefficient, $D_1$, is determined by the density of these soft modes, which varies with the exchange constant, $J$. The model further suggests an optimal density of soft modes exists at $J = J_c$, where $J_c$ represents the critical value for the 3He-Laguerre-Poisson transition. At this specific $J_c$, the soft mode density peaks, leading to the largest possible $\lim_{q \to 0} D(q)$. The text concludes by addressing the theoretical and experimental challenges associated with this soft mode density peak.

We present a hybrid semi-numerical technique to compute particle physics results that achieve both the precision of numerics and the reliability of analytic methods. This approach constructs a semi-numerical expansion of the scattering amplitude, enabling high-precision calculations of both unpolarized and polarized scattering cross sections. We validate the method through studies of various amplitudes, demonstrating its utility for implementing these calculations within the framework of MonteCarlo event generators.

We introduce **spectral channels** as a tool for characterizing and controlling light propagation in complex environments. These channels correspond directly to the eigenchannels of a system's scattering matrix, allowing for the simple expression of internal wave intenstures at specific points in terms of spectral channels' exitances (local radiative flux). The framework is validated through **Monte Carlo simulations** and verified against **3D finite-difference time-domain (FDTD)** calculations, demonstrating robust agreement. Furthermore, spectral channels offer a concise description of sources situated both inside and outside a medium and enable the **separation of optical processes** based on whether light interacts with sources internally versus externally. The primary advantage of this formalism lies in its provision of **intuitive insights** regarding radiative transfer that complement the **finite-difference time-domain** method and other traditional **transport theories**.

Our investigation utilizes a novel, data-driven approach to modeling and analyzing the complex non-thermal emission from the Milky Way, leveraging extensive datasets from the Spitzer Legacy Survey of the Galactic Center and data from various Fermi-Lite sources. This comprehensive framework, designed to handle emission across a wide frequency spectrum, reveals robust evidence for a bar structure running through the center of our galaxy and multiple high-resolution features, including spiral arms and the central bulge. Notably, our results indicate that the observed complexity in the inner regions is primarily driven by geometric effects related to the bar and spiral structures, combined with frequency-dependent differential absorption.

Multimodal optimization seeks a distribution of solutions across a broad range of fitness values rather than a single optimum, effectively generalizing both multi-objective and multi-fitness optimization problems. However, most evolutionary algorithms (NIOs) currently struggle with this task, often yielding limited diversity in the final population. This study investigates how well the SpA and the NSMO multimodal algorithms perform. Experimental results indicate that SpA successfully identifies more diverse solutions than the population size suggests, whereas NSMO's output is constrained to fewer solutions regardless of population size. Furthermore, both methods succeed in finding a broad spectrum of high-fitness solutions when the number of optima is low, but their ability to discover numerous low-fitness optima diminishes as optima density increases.

We investigate the binary matching scenario, a specialized form of the stable marriage problem, focusing on identifying a stable matching that optimizes specific matching criteria. We examine two scenarios: first, finding matchings related to utilitarian welfare (maximizing the sum of binary valuations) and, second, those linked to egalitarian welfare (maximizing the minimum stability margin). Both problems are NP-hard in polynomial time. However, we assume valuations for a case where the tasks of finding (1) a utilitarian-stable matching and (2) a lexicographically stable matching can each be solved efficiently. We provide a first demonstration that these two tasks are in P. Additionally, we present a first result showing that verifying if a given stable matching is utilitarian-stable is in P.

We investigate valley Hall transport in a suspended, armchair-edged graphene nanoribbon. By employing a tight-binding framework, we illustrate that nonuniform strain can induce both a finite Hall conductivity and anomalous transverse currents, a phenomenon attributed to the deformation of the valley Hall velocity and the emergence of a non-zero Berry connection. Our findings demonstrate that these valley Hall currents are highly sensitive to specific characteristics of the strain profile, including its spatial periodicity, overall magnitude, and direction of variation. Additionally, we reveal that modulating the width of the stress-induced mini-gaps located at the valence band maximum can effectively steer the trajectories of valley Hall currents.

Using metrics to define a center constitutes a longstanding challenge in metric geometry, often yielding multiple positive results dependent on various conditions and theoretical frameworks in literature. This paper demonstrates that every isometric subset within a positively curved space possesses a center, provided it has a nontrivial stabilizer. Centers are defined as point sets equidistant from all elements within that subset. This finding generalizes prior research by Gromov and Lytchak-Lytchak-Ruiz, which established strikng restrictions on such equal-distance set collections; the result holds across both complete and non-comprehensive metric environments.

This paper introduces a circularly polarized (CP) metamaterial-based leaky-wave antenna designed for UWB applications spanning 40–60 GHz. The proposed radiation mechanism stems from a dispersion curve bifurcation, enabled by integrating a left-handed transmission line (LHTL) with the standard radiating structure. An analysis of the CP characteristics, including UWB performance, is conducted, with measured data demonstrating a half-power beamwidth ranging from 20° to 20° and an axial ratio below 3 dB across the matched 40–55 GHz band. Furthermore, the antenna exhibits an input return loss below the -10 dB threshold throughout this frequency range, and its measured radiation efficiency is 55 percent.

Deciding which quantum operations constitute an error is a fundamental aspect of quantum error correction. Recent research suggests employing reinforcement learning (RL) within a closed-loop system to tailor these strategies specifically against noise, a concept we evaluate by integrating RL-derived approaches with quantum error detection. We assess these RL strategies against standard techniques using simulations of the surface code. Our findings reveal that the RL approach surpasses traditional methods in a non-topological framework characterized by general, non-measure-preserving error channels. However, within a topologically non-preserving context utilizing only preservation-type noise, traditional techniques prove superior. We conclude by suggesting that these RL-driven strategies may function effectively as adaptive, real-world implementations within experimental quantum systems.

Quantum jumps emerging from measurement and feedback loops present a promising avenue for meterology, enabling the precise estimation of atomic clock frequencies. This work introduces "quantum jump metrology" to track and correct atomic clock deviations using feedback, a method demonstrated via a photonic model of a two-level system driven by a misaligned laser. This framework achieves sub-Landé limit precision in such systems while surpassing conventional closed-loop "detection-and-correction" strategies by an order of magnitude or more. Notably, this "open" method operates without requiring time binning of detection events, thereby attaining optimal limit accuracy regardless of how rapidly the quantum emitter generates jumps.

Using the General-Matrix Element (GM1@LO) framework, we investigate the quark and anti-quark components of the ALICE hadron production yields in central 7.7 TeV per nucleon pair  gold- gold (Au+Au) relativistic heavy ion collisions at low transverse momentum. This framework provides next-to-leading order pQCD calculations for hard scattering quark-antiquark ($q\bar q$) production, which are then evolved down to the low transverse momentum regime using the Collins-Serperger (CS) or Mastel (MS) evolution equations. Our analysis reveals a strong dependence of the calculated anti-quark fraction on the kinematic variable $x_F$ (or equivalently, the quark momentum fraction $x$): as the $x$ value associated with the producing parton decreases, the anti-quark contribution shows a marked increase.

While quantum computers hold promise for simulating many-body systems, building large-scale architectures capable of full quantum algorithms is a long-term endeavor.
