We examine how analyzing three-body semileptonic decays of the tau leon provides insights into CP symmetry violations within the Standard Model and its extensions. Our proposed analysis focuses on tau decays involving two hadrons and a single neutrino. By comparing differential decay rate profiles of particle-antiparticle channels—specifically focusing on the momentum of an outgoing charged neutrino—we can isolate CP-violating effects. Our findings indicate that next-generation experiments, such as those planned at Belle II, could achieve a statistical precision of approximately 10^-3 in these measurements. We examine the parametrized space $\mathcal{M}_\alpha$ of $N \times N$ Tversky symmetric $p$-metrics for any parameter $\alpha \in [0,1]$, where each entry $d_{ij}$ is a non-negative value. Our analysis of the boundary of $\mathcal{M}_\alpha$ reveals that its extreme points are precisely the matrices composed of the sum of the uniform metric (all entries equal to 1) and a partition metric. A partition metric is defined as one where the space is divided into subsets by an equipartition, such that the distance between any two items in different subsets is infinite (treated here as maximal), while the distance between any two items in the same subset is zero. Deblurring is a crucial task in image processing, and recurrent deblurring methods have proven highly effective by iteratively refining the image through multiple steps. We investigate how the implementation details of inducing entangled collisions within continuous-variable atomic clocks influence the properties of the resulting atomic ensemble. The proliferation of run-time options, such as feature flags and configuration parameters, enables flexible system design but often results in optional code that remains at build time. This code incurs both direct costs in terms of memory and CPU cycle consumption, as well as indirect risks where features may leak into production despite being disabled in the run-time, leading to system instability. Although this overhead is frequently negligible, it can be significant for resource-constrained, real-time systems used in robotics, automotive applications, and medical devices, where every byte and processor unit counts. Consequently, there is an urgent need to automatically identify and remove over-head generated by inactive run-time options to enhance system performance and reliability, a process this work frames as Static Run-Time Option Removal (SRRP). We establish a formal approach to define SRR methods and present OptionPruner, the inaugural automatic tool that performs SRR via control-flow analysis. Testing the OptionPruner on 11 industrial case studies, the tool demonstrated a capacity to eliminate between 10% and 95% of the memory and CPU time associated with unused options, with the majority of these options previously going undetected. Furthermore, extensive manual verification by a panel of 11 software engineers confirmed that the removal operations performed did not compromise the correctness of the software.

This work investigates dark matter (DM) interactions with atomic nuclei, resulting in bound-state transitions within the nucleus, mediated by a vector mediator that couples to both the current of charged leptons and to the current of fermionic constituents inside the nucleon. This paper introduces an unsupervised deep-learning technique designed to derive inter-beat intervals (IBIs) from noisy electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. Notably, this approach operates without requiring ground-truth IBBs for training the deep-learning network. Experimental results demonstrate strong agreement between algorithm-generated IBBs and reference values from ground-truth sources.

This conclusion holds effectively even when non-vanarity is considered to a large extent. Existing multilingual models are built upon pre-knowledge from multiple sources; however, this creates an urgent need for further multilingual pre-training. Notably, the multilingual Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoupling module prevents module imbalances, while the Multi-head Cross-lingual Attention (MCA) module enhances cross-lingual capabilities. In reinforcement learning (RL), a persistent challenge involves efficiently transferring knowledge across multiple tasks. Current and upcoming gravitational-wave interferometers will detect mergers of compact binaries with total masses spanning from $0.1$ to hundreds of solar masses. While current observational data and estimates from standard stellar evolution suggest that most detectable binaries possess moderate spins and high eccentricities, the characteristics of sources within the detector's sensitive frequency band ($f_{\rm det}$) cannot be directly inferred from properties at larger orbital separations ($f \ll f_{\rm det}$). This is because General Relativity (GR) and chromphoronic tidal interactions significantly alter orbital eccentricity and semi-major axis as binaries evolve toward coalescence. This study quantifies these final eccentricities for binaries comprising objects with zero to unit spin, covering spin-orbit misorientations from aligned to anti-aligned, within mass ranges relevant to present and near-future detection capabilities. Consequently, the inferred eccentricity distribution of detectable sources will likely be bimodal, featuring one mode for binaries with constituent masses below $2\,\rm M_\odot$ and another for heavier components. These findings offer critical constraints for gravitational-wave data analysis and provide insights into the formation channels of compact object pairs.

Dynamic graph event detection is a critical component of event processing, yet existing methods often struggle with insufficient modeling of temporal evolution and sparse inter-prerequisite links between events, particularly in noisy environments. To address these challenges, we introduce DyGED, a Multi-instance Multi-label (MML) framework designed for precise event discovery in dynamic graphs. Unlike traditional single-instance single-label (S1S1) approaches that struggle with graph sparsity, DyGED treats each time step in a dynamic graph as a distinct instance, effectively capturing recurrence and the full label set for precise detection. The model integrates two primary mechanisms: first, a Time-aware Graph Evolution Network (T-GEvN) that captures both short- and long-term dependencies through multi-scale temporal sliding windows and self-attention; second, a Sparsely Connected Label Imputation (SC-LI) module that leverages the Label Dependency Graph (L-DG) to fill in missing prerequisites, thereby mitigating sparsity. Empirical evaluations across three real-world datasets confirm that DyGED significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, ablation studies highlight the efficacy of its multi-instance multi-label design, SC-LI, and the T-GEvN.

Lindblad dynamics, defined as the most general class of Markovian quantum open system evolution, drive the asymptotic approach of systems toward Gaussian states. We present a reduced kinetic model designed to simulate island coalescence within the tokamak scrape-off layer, offering a bridge between large-scale magnetohydrodynamics and the underlying kinetics. By reducing the computationally expensive full Vlasov equation to depend only on magnetic flux surfaces, the extent of necessary numerical resolution is significantly curtailed. This reduction allows essential features of the distribution function to be expressed in terms of adiabatic invariants, enabling the incorporation of full kinetic effects that standard fluid descriptions typically miss. Furthermore, by adjusting the collision operator, specific facets of the micro-meso interaction can be isolated. Initial tests confirm the validity of this reduced framework, validating its capacity to function as an effective link in the broader context of magnetohydrodynamic stability.

How come digital helpers like customer service bots can quickly grasp complex tasks alongside humans, even lacking the human capacity for long-term collaborative learning? This paper introduces "collaborative lifelong learning" (CLL), a multi-agent framework enabling both artificial intelligence systems and humans to co-develop cognitive strategies, refined structures, and intuitive insights across an ongoing sequence of interactions. Our approach merges principles from imitation learning, social bandits, reinforcement learning, neural architecture search, and social learning into a cohesive solution. CLL equips multi-agent networks with the capability to construct, refine, and iteratively apply agent architectures optimized for specific tasks over extended partnerships with human operators. Validated through extensive testing across diverse task scenarios and partner configurations, our results demonstrate that CLL yields highly agent- and human-specific, task-optimized architectures capable of delivering exceptional performance.
